sourceNotes: Seeded from BSM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: BSM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: An uptime promise of 99.99%, which allows only 52.6 minutes of unplanned outage a year — about 4.4 minutes a month — against the 8.8 hours a 99.9% tier permits.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client in a business-services roleplay demands a tighter guarantee, you have to convert each tier into allowed downtime minutes before you can price the upgrade or refuse it.

terms.definition: The period over which uptime is averaged before credits are computed; a four-hour outage breaches a daily window but disappears inside a monthly average, so the window length decides whether the same failure costs the vendor anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward the competitor who asks how availability is measured rather than only what percentage is promised, because the window is where a generous-looking SLA is quietly defanged.

terms.definition: A contractual clock that runs until the client's issue is actually fixed rather than merely acknowledged, so a vendor can meet a 15-minute acknowledgement promise and still breach a four-hour fix promise on the same ticket.
terms.whyItMatters: Support-contract roleplays hinge on separating the two clocks; quoting one response number when the client is complaining about repair speed reads as evasion to a judge.

terms.definition: Hours charged to clients divided by hours available in the period; on a 2,000-hour year a consultant at 75% bills 1,500 hours, so each point lost is roughly 20 hours of revenue that cannot be recovered later.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and hiring questions on a services exam are settled with this ratio — you cannot argue for another consultant without showing the current team's utilization.

terms.definition: Dollars actually collected divided by the dollars standard rates would have produced; a firm billing 1,500 hours at $200 but collecting $255,000 realizes 85%, with the gap made of write-offs, courtesy hours and negotiated discounts.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains the exam scenario where a fully booked practice still misses its revenue target — the hours were worked and utilization was fine, but they were not all billed.

terms.definition: Client price divided by the delivery staffer's fully loaded cost rate — a $50 cost billed at $150 is a 3.0 multiple, roughly the floor a services firm needs to cover overhead, bench time and still earn a profit.
terms.whyItMatters: A discount request in a B2B selling roleplay is answered with this number: cutting a $150 rate to $110 drops the multiple to 2.2 and eats the margin the firm runs on.

terms.definition: The mix of junior to senior staff carrying an engagement; pushing work down a level lifts margin because juniors bill somewhat less but cost far less, which is why a pyramid-shaped team beats an all-expert team on the same fixed fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing a fixed-fee project in a roleplay means defending the mix to a client who wants only senior people on the account.

terms.definition: A surety instrument worth roughly 5% to 10% of the amount bid, forfeited if the winning bidder walks away or refuses to sign at the price submitted, which is what makes a lowball number costly to withdraw.
terms.whyItMatters: Public-sector and large corporate solicitations require one, so a roleplay about pursuing a government services contract has to account for its cost in the bid decision.

terms.definition: Chained dependencies multiply rather than average, so a service running on a 99.9% platform behind a 99.9% network and a 99.95% payment gateway can honestly promise only 99.75% end to end — roughly 22 hours of outage a year.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants 99.9% guaranteed on a stack you resell is answered by multiplying your vendors' numbers first; promising more than the product is a breach you signed at the outset.

terms.definition: The downtime a target permits, treated as an allowance to spend rather than a line to defend — a 99.9% monthly promise leaves 43.2 minutes, so one 20-minute release failure has already consumed nearly half the month.
terms.whyItMatters: Change-management items on a services exam use it as the trigger: once the budget is spent the vendor freezes releases, which is the concrete answer to when you stop shipping.

terms.definition: Average elapsed time from detection to the service being usable again, and the lever inside availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR); with a failure every 500 hours, cutting restoration from four hours to one moves uptime from 99.2% to 99.8%.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client demands fewer outages in a managed-services roleplay, faster recovery is the cheaper counter-offer, and you need the formula to prove it lands on the same uptime number.

terms.definition: Banded refunds tied to the month's measured uptime — 99.0 to 99.9% returns 10% of the fee, 95 to 99% returns 25%, under 95% returns 50% — so a month at 98.7% on a $40,000 contract owes $10,000 and the band edge, not the outage length, sets the bill.
terms.whyItMatters: Renewal negotiations turn on which band an outage lands in; a competitor who can price the month before conceding a credit keeps the account profitable.

terms.definition: The hours during which response clocks actually run: under 8x5 coverage a severity-one ticket opened at 4 p.m. Friday with a four-hour target is not late until Monday noon, while the identical promise under 24x7 breaches at 8 p.m.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in a support-contract roleplay watch for the competitor who sells the coverage upgrade rather than a tighter number — the clock's hours, not its length, are what the client is complaining about.

terms.definition: Total support spend divided by tickets resolved, a figure that rises when self-service succeeds, because the cheap contacts are the ones deflected and the expensive escalated ones are all that remain in the denominator.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where automation raised cost per ticket is testing whether you read the mix change instead of calling the deflection program a failure.

terms.definition: Cash actually received divided by the amount invoiced — a different fraction from realization, because a firm can bill 95% of standard rates and still collect only 80% of those invoices, and only the second number funds payroll.
terms.whyItMatters: A cash-squeeze roleplay at a fully booked agency is solved here: the repair is in collections and credit terms, not in selling more hours.

terms.definition: Salary plus payroll taxes, benefits and allocated overhead, divided by the hours a person is genuinely available to bill rather than the 2,080 they are paid for; using the payroll denominator understates true cost by roughly 15 to 20% and prices work below breakeven.
terms.whyItMatters: Every pricing-floor question on a services exam starts here, and quoting a bill rate off unloaded salary in a roleplay ends the sale as soon as a judge asks about benefits.

terms.definition: Signed but undelivered revenue divided by average monthly delivery capacity, read in months — under about three months a firm is hiring into hope, and over six it is quietly turning away work it could have sold.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring recommendation in a business-services roleplay needs this number, because "we're busy" is not evidence a judge accepts for adding headcount.

terms.definition: Hours already delivered but not yet invoiced; add the days they sit unbilled to the days an invoice waits for payment and a monthly billing cycle on net-45 terms funds about 75 days of payroll before the first dollar arrives.
terms.whyItMatters: The cash-flow roleplay at a growing consultancy is won by shortening the billing cycle, which only makes sense once unbilled days and receivable days are counted as one lag.

terms.definition: Booking a share of a fixed fee equal to costs incurred over total estimated costs, which means an overrun mechanically pulls revenue forward: spend 70% of the budget on half the work and the books show 70% earned until the estimate is revised and it reverses.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions about a services firm restating a quarter test whether you know the cost estimate, not the invoice, drives when revenue lands.

terms.definition: Forecast final cost of an engagement: money already spent plus the remaining work divided by the cost performance index, so $60,000 spent with $40,000 of work left at a CPI of 0.8 finishes at $110,000, not the $100,000 in the proposal.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-project roleplays where the client asks whether the budget still holds require this arithmetic before you promise anything you cannot deliver.

terms.definition: Revenue on one project less only its direct delivery cost — loaded labor, travel and subcontractors — before any overhead, so a 40% result at a firm carrying a 35% overhead load leaves five points and is a project worth declining.
terms.whyItMatters: A go/no-go roleplay on a discounted proposal turns on comparing this margin against the overhead load, not on whether the project appears to make money.

terms.definition: The agreed fee divided by the hours the team actually consumed: $48,000 delivered in 320 hours is $150 an hour against a $200 rate card, a 25% erosion that never appears in revenue and shows up only when delivered hours are counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Post-project debriefs on the services exam ask why a profitable-looking fixed fee hurt the year, and this ratio is the evidence a judge expects you to produce.

terms.definition: The hour count at which two pricing structures cost the buyer the same — a $60,000 fee against a $200 blended rate breaks even at 300 hours — so a client whose scope truly needs 250 should refuse the fixed price and one expecting 400 should insist on it.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing roleplays are decided by naming that crossover out loud; recommending a structure without it reads as a preference rather than analysis.

terms.definition: A prepaid bank of hours billed at a discount and forfeited if unused inside the period, unlike an access retainer that buys availability whether or not any work is requested — the expiry, not the discount, is the term worth negotiating.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking to roll over unused hours at renewal is asking you to change which retainer they bought, so you have to know the two are different products before conceding.

terms.definition: Payment set as a share of verified savings above an agreed baseline, which means whoever defines the baseline defines the payout — anchor it on a peak-cost year and the vendor earns a bonus for the client merely reverting to normal spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Outsourcing roleplays that open with "we only pay if you save us money" are won by negotiating the baseline and the measurement method, never the percentage.

terms.definition: A fee computed as a fixed share of whatever the job ends up costing, which pays the provider more for every overrun and is barred outright in federal contracting for exactly that reason; a fee fixed in dollars at award is the lawful version.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-services roleplays require pricing the work in a structure the buyer may legally accept — proposing a percentage of cost disqualifies the bid before the price is compared.

terms.definition: The smallest unit a ticket can bill in, and at a quarter-hour floor forty six-minute calls invoice ten hours against four actually worked, which is why increment size rather than hourly rate often decides whether a support contract earns anything.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing an invoice in a roleplay is usually disputing the increment, so you have to reconstruct the bill from ticket counts to answer them.

terms.definition: An endorsement extending the reporting period after a claims-made professional liability policy ends, priced near 100 to 200% of the last annual premium; skip it and work already delivered becomes uninsured the moment the policy lapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling or winding down a services firm in a roleplay means budgeting for it, because past clients can still sue and the buyer's diligence list asks for proof it was purchased.

terms.definition: A smaller cap sitting inside a larger one for a named category of loss, so a $5 million cyber policy carrying a $250,000 social-engineering sublimit pays a quarter of a million on a wire-fraud loss no matter what the headline limit says.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client's contract demands $5 million of cyber coverage, the roleplay answer is to read the sublimits, because that is where the protection they actually need is rationed.

terms.definition: The most an insurer will pay across every claim in a policy year, a separate ceiling from the per-occurrence cap — a $1 million / $2 million policy that pays two full claims in March leaves the client uncovered for the remaining nine months.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-qualification roleplay where the client requires $1 million of errors-and-omissions coverage is answered with both numbers; meeting the per-occurrence figure alone can leave the contract effectively bare.

terms.definition: Card-transaction volume decides which validation a provider must pass: above roughly six million a year forces an on-site assessment by a qualified assessor plus quarterly network scans, while a small e-commerce seller self-assesses on a questionnaire.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-adjacent services roleplay hinges on whether absorbing a client's volume pushes you over the threshold, because the compliance cost, not the processing fee, is what changes.

terms.definition: A signed statement covering the gap between an audit report's period end and the client's fiscal year end — a report closing September 30 needs one for October through December, and most auditors refuse to bridge more than about three months.
terms.whyItMatters: Enterprise procurement roleplays stall exactly here: the client's auditor wants assurance through December and the vendor's only report stops in September.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: Marketing through online channels such as social media, email, and search.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital promotion reaches audiences efficiently with measurable results.

terms.definition: Damping an emotion after it has already arrived by hiding its outward signs, rather than changing the interpretation that produced it. Because it is applied late, it leaves the physiological arousal fully intact, raises blood pressure in the person watching as well, and measurably impairs memory for what was said during the episode -- the opposite profile from cognitive reappraisal, which is applied early and carries none of those costs.
terms.whyItMatters: When a Human Resources Management Series judge asks how you would hold composure while an employee vents about a denied raise, an answer built on hiding what you felt names the strategy research links to worse recall of the conversation; the scoring answer reinterprets the outburst before it peaks.

terms.definition: The step under UCC Article 9 that makes a creditor's claim to collateral good against other creditors and a bankruptcy trustee, accomplished most often by filing a UCC-1 financing statement with the state and sometimes by possession or control of the collateral. Attachment alone binds only the debtor; among competing perfected creditors priority runs first to file or perfect, so the lender who files first outranks the lender who lent first.
terms.whyItMatters: Debtor-creditor roleplays with two lenders claiming the same equipment are resolved by filing date, never by loan date.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: Rewards total volume purchased across a stated period, so a buyer's separate orders add together toward the break. A noncumulative discount resets with every order, which is why the cumulative form builds account loyalty while the noncumulative one is far easier to defend as cost-justified under Robinson-Patman.
terms.whyItMatters: Distributor roleplays ask which discount structure stops an account from splitting its orders among three suppliers, and the two forms give opposite answers.

terms.definition: The emotional and rational reasons a customer makes a purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding motives helps position products around what matters.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: A structured idea session run in four fixed stages: members write ideas silently and independently, then a round-robin in which each person contributes one idea per turn with no discussion allowed, then clarification of each posted item, then private ranking whose tally decides the outcome. Silent generation and one-at-a-time posting are what separate it from open brainstorming, where the loudest member anchors the room; the Delphi technique goes further by keeping experts anonymous across written rounds so they never meet at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Problem-solving group items ask which method protects the quiet member's idea, and this is the process that names how.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Clicks divided by impressions: 250 clicks on 125,000 impressions is 0.2%, which is an ordinary display result and a poor search result. The denominator is impressions served, not people reached, so the figure falls as frequency rises even when the creative is working.
terms.whyItMatters: Campaign-review roleplays hand over a rate that dropped week over week; the competitor is expected to check whether frequency rose before concluding the creative went stale.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: State laws capping increases on essentials once a disaster or emergency is formally declared, many of them fixing a numeric trigger such as more than 10% above the pre-emergency price or above the seller's own documented cost increase. There is no federal counterpart, so legality depends on the state and on the declaration being in force.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics question about raising generator prices during a hurricane tests whether the competitor knows the trigger is the declared emergency, not merely a high price.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Total quota handed out across the sales force divided by the revenue the company actually forecasts. Assigning 1.1 to 1.3 times the target is deliberate over-assignment that absorbs ramping reps, mid-year attrition and under-performers, so the plan still lands if some reps miss — it measures quota against target, where pipeline coverage measures open deals against quota.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay that asks you to set quotas for next year is scored on whether you over-assign on purpose and can say why; the exam pairs this with pipeline coverage to see if you can tell the two ratios apart.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: The specific group a promotional message is designed to reach.
terms.whyItMatters: Defining the audience shapes the message, media, and timing.

terms.definition: A financial statement reporting the cash flowing into and out of a business over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash flow reveals whether a business can pay its bills even when it reports a profit.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: Varies price and allocates a fixed, perishable capacity across booking classes so the highest-paying demand can still be served late - airline seats, hotel rooms, rental cars. Dynamic pricing simply moves the number with demand, whereas here the binding constraint is capacity that expires worthless at a deadline and cannot be inventoried.
terms.whyItMatters: A lodging roleplay about a sold-out weekend expects the candidate to hold rooms back for late high-rate bookings instead of filling the house early at a discount.

terms.definition: Closed-won revenue divided by the number of deals won — $480,000 across 60 wins is $8,000 each. It measures one whole customer agreement, where average order value measures one transaction, so a customer who reorders four times a year raises order count without raising this figure at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking you to justify spending more selling time per account is answered by comparing deal size against cost per sales call, not by citing total revenue.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: A documented escalation applied to correctable conduct — typically verbal warning, written warning, final written warning or suspension, then termination — with each step recorded, dated and acknowledged so the record shows notice was given. It is deliberately bypassed for gross misconduct such as theft, violence or safety sabotage, where immediate termination is appropriate, and skipping steps for ordinary conduct is what makes a later discharge look pretextual.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay about a chronically late employee is scored on naming the step reached and what documentation exists, not on describing a conversation.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: Groups buyers by what they measurably did — purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty status, benefit sought — read from transaction records, while psychographic segmentation groups them by what they say they value and geographic segmentation by where they live; a heavy user and a light user can match on every demographic and psychographic trait and still belong in different behavioral segments, so it is the only base that predicts volume directly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty-program roleplays ask which customers to reward; the winning answer segments on measured usage rate rather than on who the customers are.

terms.definition: The combination of hardware, software, data, and people used to collect, process, store, and share information.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding systems is key when competitors evaluate technology investments.

terms.definition: An item deliberately priced at or below cost to pull traffic that then buys higher-margin goods. Roughly half the states police the tactic through unfair sales acts requiring a minimum markup over cost, often near 6% at retail, and it stays lawful because it lacks the recoupment intent that makes predatory pricing actionable.
terms.whyItMatters: Grocery and drugstore roleplays ask a candidate to defend a below-cost milk price to a judge who suspects the practice is illegal.

terms.definition: Every open deal multiplied by the win probability its current stage carries, then summed. A $200,000 deal sitting in a 30 percent stage counts as $60,000, so $1.4 million of raw pipeline spread across early stages may weight to under $400,000 — the total becomes a forecast instead of a list of what is theoretically in play.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting items give a table of deal values and stage probabilities and expect the weighted total, not the sum; in a roleplay defending a forecast to a manager, quoting raw pipeline reads as the rookie answer.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: Launching into a different product category under an existing brand name — Dove soap into Dove shampoo — whereas a line extension adds a variant inside the category the brand already sells, such as another Dove soap scent; the category jump risks diluting what the parent name means, while the in-category variant mainly risks stealing volume from its own siblings, so the two carry different failure modes and different tests.
terms.whyItMatters: Product roleplays that hand you a growth mandate are scored on naming which of the two you chose and the specific risk it carries; treating them as the same move loses both points.

terms.definition: Offers the components both individually and as a discounted package, so a buyer may take one piece alone or the whole set. Pure bundling removes the standalone option entirely, which extracts more from buyers who value the pieces evenly but loses every customer who wants only one of them.
terms.whyItMatters: Fast-food and software roleplays about a value meal or a suite ask which of the two forms fits a customer base with mixed preferences.

terms.definition: Purchase price plus installation, training, consumables, maintenance and downtime across the asset's life, minus its resale value — so a $12,000 machine burning $400 of supplies a year beats a $9,000 machine burning $1,600 within five years. It answers a price objection by moving the comparison from acquisition price to lifetime cost.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer says a competitor quoted less, judges look for this calculation rather than a discount, because conceding on price is the response the rubric marks down.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining relationships with professionals to exchange knowledge and opportunity.
terms.whyItMatters: Networking is essential for discovering and advancing career opportunities.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: The measured pattern in which unit cost falls by a constant percentage each time cumulative output doubles — an 80% curve means the 200th unit costs 80% of the 100th — so the advantage belongs to accumulated experience, not to current period volume as in economies of scale.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a starting unit cost and a curve percentage and expect the cost after a doubling, so the arithmetic has to be known and not just the idea that practice helps.

terms.definition: Share of respondents who name a brand when asked only to list the brands they can think of in a category with nothing shown to them, as opposed to aided awareness, where the interviewer reads the name and the respondent only confirms recognition; aided scores typically run two to four times higher than unaided ones, so the two measures can never be compared with each other or with a competitor's differently-worded question.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand you awareness research want you to challenge the number's basis before acting on it; treating an aided figure as proof of strong awareness is the standard trap.

terms.definition: A price reduction or payment a manufacturer gives a reseller in exchange for performing an advertising or display function - a co-op ad, an end-cap, a feature in the weekly circular. Robinson-Patman requires it be made available on proportionally equal terms to all competing customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-negotiation roleplays ask what the retailer owes in return for the money, and the answer is a performed service rather than simply a larger order.

terms.definition: Ramped headcount times individual quota times the attainment rate the team really achieves — 20 reps carrying $500,000 each but hitting 70 percent supports $7 million of revenue, not the $10 million the quota sheet implies. Skipping the attainment factor is what makes a hiring plan promise revenue the team has never once delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: A growth-planning roleplay that asks how many reps to hire to reach a revenue goal is graded on multiplying in historical attainment; the exam tests it as a three-factor calculation.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: Two firms at the SAME channel stage pooling capital, production or distribution to chase an opportunity neither could take alone — a coffee brand operating kiosks inside a bookstore chain. A vertical marketing system, by contrast, joins firms at DIFFERENT stages of the same channel under one owner, contract or dominant member.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and marketing roleplays that propose a co-branded partnership are graded on naming this structure and the fact that neither partner is the other's supplier.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: Invoice terms granting a 2% discount if the bill is paid within 10 days, with the full amount due on day 30. Passing it up is costly: (2 / 98) x (365 / 20) works out near 37% a year, which is why forgone cash discounts are treated as one of the most expensive sources of short-term funds a business can use.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-terms roleplay asks whether to borrow in order to take the discount, and the annualized figure is what convinces the judge either way.

terms.definition: A plan outlining the method, variables, population, and analysis for a study.
terms.whyItMatters: Design choices decide whether research answers the business question.

terms.definition: Diagnosing the buyer's problem through questioning and recommending the right fit even when that means a smaller order, as against transactional selling, which moves a known item at speed and treats the exchange as complete at the register. The dividing line is who defines the need: the buyer arrives with it in a transaction, the rep uncovers it here.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer asks for a product that will not solve their stated problem, the rubric credits the competitor who redirects the recommendation over the one who rings up the request.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: The status that exposes a business to cleanup costs under the Superfund statute (CERCLA), reaching four groups: current owners or operators of a contaminated site, owners at the time of disposal, parties who arranged for disposal of the waste, and transporters who selected the site. Liability is strict, retroactive to conduct that was lawful when it happened, and joint and several, so one solvent party can be billed for the whole cleanup; the innocent-landowner defense requires all appropriate inquiry before purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Environmental-law roleplays about buying a former dry-cleaning site explain why the site assessment happens before closing, not after.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: What the buyer actually owes after every trade, quantity and cash discount has come off the list figure. List price is the published starting point and the invoice price is what the seller bills before payment terms are applied, so all three numbers can differ on a single order.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing roleplays hand a competitor a list price plus a stack of discounts and ask what the check will actually be written for.

terms.definition: Count of deals where the buyer bought nothing at all, divided by all closed-lost deals — not by all opportunities. If 60 of 100 losses were no-decisions, the problem is urgency and the business case, because a buyer who chose a rival was at least persuaded to purchase; splitting losses this way points at two completely different fixes.
terms.whyItMatters: A win-loss review roleplay is scored on separating the two loss types before recommending anything, and the exam plants a competitor-versus-status-quo distinction in the stem.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Standard structures for business documents such as memos, reports, and proposals.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the correct format for each document type.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: A series of trade discounts taken one after another off list: 30/20/10 means 70% of list, then 80% of that, then 90% of that, for a net factor of 0.504 rather than the 40% of list that adding the rates would suggest. These compensate channel members for functions performed, unlike a cash discount, which rewards only speed of payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesale-quote roleplays hand a competitor a stacked discount and ask for the net price, and adding the percentages together is precisely the error being tested.

terms.definition: A short-window, fixed-dollar bonus paid per unit on one targeted product — $50 a unit for 30 days, frequently funded by the manufacturer and paid outside the regular commission plan. An accelerator instead lifts the commission percentage on everything sold past quota, so one steers which item gets pushed and the other rewards total volume.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selling items describe a vendor paying a retailer's floor staff per unit and ask what the payment is; a promotion roleplay expects you to name the mechanism that redirects selling effort to one slow-moving SKU.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: The specific actions and tools used to carry out a marketing strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Tactics turn strategy into concrete, executable actions.

terms.definition: A shortcut that estimates how many years an investment takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays reward a competitor who can tell a client on the spot that 8% doubles their money in about nine years.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: Rooms revenue / rooms available, which is the same as average daily rate multiplied by occupancy percentage. Because it charges the property for its empty rooms, it exposes the trade-off that ADR alone hides: a rate cut that fills the house can raise this figure even while the average rate falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about discounting a slow midweek are settled by comparing this metric against ADR rather than by looking at the room rate on its own.

terms.definition: Quantifying the buyer's gain in the buyer's own numbers — hours saved times loaded labor rate, or scrap avoided times unit cost — so the proposal shows a payback period instead of a feature list. Feature-benefit selling states what a feature does for the customer; this states what that outcome is worth in dollars per year.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business roleplays that give you the client's volumes and costs are asking for a dollar case, and a competitor who only lists benefits leaves the quantified point unscored.

terms.term: Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA)
terms.definition: Guarantees reemployment to a worker returning from military service, capped at five years of cumulative absence from one employer, with the return application due within 1 day for service under 31 days, 14 days for service of 31 to 180 days, and 90 days beyond that. The escalator principle puts the returning worker in the position they would have reached had they never left, not merely the job they held on departure.
terms.whyItMatters: A reinstatement roleplay is scored on the escalator principle — offering the old job back at the old pay is the wrong answer when promotions occurred meanwhile.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: A written table stating how long each class of record is kept and when it must be destroyed, built on statutory floors rather than preference: the IRS's ordinary three-year assessment window, seven years for records supporting a bad-debt or worthless-securities claim, and the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that audit work papers survive seven years.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-records roleplay asks how long the storeroom keeps signed invoices before shredding them, and a judge expects a statutory minimum, not a guess like 'a few years'.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: The amount or percentage added to a product's cost to set its selling price.
terms.whyItMatters: Markup links cost directly to a pricing recommendation.

terms.definition: The FTC rule confining outbound sales calls to a residence to the hours between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. in the customer's local time zone, and requiring the caller to state who is calling, what is being sold and the total cost before taking any payment. A New York center dialing California at 8:30 p.m. Eastern is legal because the customer's clock reads 5:30 p.m.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items plant a two-time-zone call and ask whether it is lawful, which is decided by the customer's local hour; an outbound-calling roleplay expects the disclosure sequence before any card number is requested.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: A measure of how much customer demand responds to a price change.
terms.whyItMatters: Elasticity predicts demand shifts and helps optimize price for revenue.

terms.definition: Licensing threshold most states impose on CPA candidates: 150 semester hours of college credit — 30 beyond the 120 a bachelor's degree typically carries — plus all four sections of the Uniform CPA Exam and a year of supervised experience. Several states now allow a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience as an alternate route to the same license.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting-designations roleplay asks what a college junior must still complete before licensure; the answer is a credit count and an exam, not a job offer.

terms.definition: Placing the product in the customer's hands for a free trial, test drive or home-approval period and letting possession persuade, because giving the item back later registers as a loss. A takeaway close works from the opposite direction, threatening to withdraw the offer or the model rather than handing it over.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and automotive roleplays with a hesitant buyer reward a named trial-based close, and pairing it with the store's return policy shows you know the company's selling rules.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: A goal system pairing one qualitative objective with three to five numeric key results scored 0.0 to 1.0, where roughly 0.7 is the intended landing point for stretch goals; unlike a KPI, which monitors an ongoing business rate, each key result is a quarter-long target that expires.
terms.whyItMatters: Written management events ask you to convert a vague team aim into measurable targets, and the graders look for the numeric key results and the scoring interpretation.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: The percentage of revenue left as profit after costs are subtracted.
terms.whyItMatters: Margin reflects pricing effectiveness against financial goals.

terms.definition: Sellers must re-scrub their calling lists against the federal registry at least every 31 days, and may reach a listed consumer only through an existing business relationship — 18 months after that person's last purchase, or 3 months after an inquiry — or with signed written permission. A list bought once and used for a year fails the scrub requirement no matter how it was sourced.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a purchase date and a call date and ask whether the relationship exemption still covers the call; a prospecting roleplay is scored on saying how often the list is cleaned.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: One member's ability to make another do what it otherwise would not, drawn from the five French-and-Raven bases: coercive (threatening to cut supply or shelf space), reward (extra margin or funds), expert (knowledge the other lacks), referent (the partner wants the association), and legitimate (a contract already requires it). Coercive power gets compliance but raises conflict; referent and expert power get cooperation.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-relationship roleplay asks how you would move a resistant distributor; naming the base you are using, and why coercion would cost you the relationship, is the scored discrimination.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
