terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: The percentage of respondents answering 9 or 10 on an eleven-point recommendation question minus the percentage answering 0 through 6, with the 7s and 8s discarded entirely, producing a figure that can run from -100 to +100; because the middle is dropped, a respectable score of 30 can still conceal a large block of detractors.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where management reports a score of 30 as good needs the formula unpacked, because the discarded middle and the detractor share are where the action is.

terms.definition: Expresses the dollar markup as a percentage of what the merchandise cost the seller: (retail - cost) / cost. A $40 item ticketed at $100 carries a 150% markup on cost but only a 60% markup on retail; convert between them with markup-on-retail = markup-on-cost / (1 + markup-on-cost).
terms.whyItMatters: Merchandising math items hand a competitor one percentage and ask for the other selling price, and dividing by retail when the problem said cost throws off every later step of the calculation.

terms.definition: Total pay a rep receives at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus variable pay at plan, so a $60,000 base with $60,000 of commission at plan is $120,000 at a 50/50 pay mix. It is a plan figure and not a promise: only the base half is paid regardless of results, which is what separates it from a salary.
terms.whyItMatters: A recruiting roleplay that pitches a sales job is scored on explaining the split honestly, and quoting the total as if it were guaranteed is an ethical mark against you.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The process section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act requires before an agency may issue a binding legislative rule: publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, take public comment for a stated period, respond to the significant comments, and publish the final rule with a statement of basis and purpose, normally effective 30 days later. A rule adopted without those steps can be vacated as procedurally invalid even when its substance is sound.
terms.whyItMatters: Administrative-law questions ask how an industry trade group can influence a regulation before it ever binds its members.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: A plan for setting prices to meet business objectives and positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: A sound strategy is central to case presentations and positioning.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring prior express written consent — signed, specific to marketing contact, and not made a condition of buying anything — before an autodialer or prerecorded message may call or text a mobile number, and requiring every seller to keep its own internal do-not-call list for five years. A checkbox buried in a purchase flow does not meet the standard.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-selling roleplay on texting a prospect list is graded on whether you ask how consent was captured; exam items contrast a consumer who bought something with one who signed a marketing permission.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 index of how far a society's less powerful members accept unequal distribution of authority - Malaysia scores near 100, Austria near 11, the United States around 40. It is a separate dimension from individualism: a high-power-distance audience expects the most senior person to speak first, treats public disagreement with a manager as an attack, and takes an invitation to challenge the presenter as a trap, so a presentation that works in a low-index room must be restructured rather than merely translated.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to adapt a pitch for an overseas client, the scored answer changes who presents and how questions are invited, not just the language.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Sets the average category buyer's annual purchase volume at 1.00 and states a brand's buyers against it, so 1.30 means the people who choose this brand buy 30% more of the category per year than the typical buyer; it is the third multiplier that converts a penetration figure and a repeat rate into a share estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the factor students silently drop from a share forecast, turning a 12% answer into 10%, and it is the evidence behind a plan that argues for targeting heavy users instead of chasing more triers.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: Divides the same dollar markup by the selling price instead of by the cost: (retail - cost) / retail. It is the form buyers and merchandise plans quote, it always reads lower than the cost-based figure on the same item, and it converts back with markup-on-cost = markup-on-retail / (1 - markup-on-retail).
terms.whyItMatters: In a retail-buying roleplay a judge states margins the way the trade states them, so a candidate has to convert a vendor's quoted markup before comparing it to the store's own target.

terms.definition: Adding a product from a different category to the purchase — a case bought with a laptop — while upselling moves the customer up within the same line to a larger or higher-grade version of what they already chose. Suggestive selling covers both from the counter; the line that separates these two is category versus tier.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays scored on add-on sales ask you to name and demonstrate the technique, and calling a larger size a cross-sell is the error judges catch immediately.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: The rate applied to the next dollar earned, which is the top bracket a taxpayer reaches rather than the rate paid on all of their income.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-liability items test whether a raise into a higher bracket taxes the whole salary at the new rate — it does not, only the dollars above the bracket line.

terms.definition: Total marketing spend divided by net sales, times 100 — programs, salaries, agency fees and campaigns, not just media — so it answers what the plan costs to run. Marketing ROI asks the opposite question, what the same spend returned.
terms.whyItMatters: Control questions ask which metric shows a plan is over budget versus which shows it was unprofitable; naming the wrong one loses the item even when the arithmetic is right.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged. The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: The retail convention of doubling delivered cost, so a $22 cost gets a $44 ticket. That one move is simultaneously a 100% markup on cost and exactly a 50% markup on retail, which is why the same practice gets quoted as two different percentages depending on the denominator.
terms.whyItMatters: Apparel and specialty-store pricing cases open with keystone as the starting ticket, then ask what margin survives after the item is marked down twice.

terms.definition: The employment eligibility verification record required of every U.S. employer by the Immigration Reform and Control Act: the employee completes Section 1 no later than the first day of work for pay, and the employer examines original documents and completes Section 2 within three business days of that start. The form is retained three years after hire or one year after termination, whichever is later, and is kept apart from the personnel file.
terms.whyItMatters: An onboarding roleplay that lists paperwork must place this inside the three-business-day window, a deadline competitors routinely confuse with the first payroll run.

terms.definition: Federal postal law lets anyone who receives goods they never ordered keep them as a free gift, with no duty to pay and no duty to ship them back, and a follow-up invoice creates no obligation. Only free samples plainly marked as such and merchandise sent by a charity asking for a donation fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items describe a company mailing a product with a bill attached and ask what the recipient owes; a customer-complaint roleplay expects you to tell the caller the item is theirs.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: An instruction that suspends the retention schedule and freezes every document touching anticipated or filed litigation, overriding routine destruction until counsel lifts it; skipping it exposes the company to spoliation sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) even when the deletion was only the ordinary schedule running as designed.
terms.whyItMatters: In a legal-issues roleplay where a customer has threatened suit, the first correct action is stopping automatic email deletion — not gathering documents after the subpoena arrives.

terms.definition: Continuing to fund a failing course of action in order to justify having chosen it. The dividing line from the sunk-cost fallacy is who is deciding: sunk cost is the reasoning error of counting unrecoverable spend at all, and anyone can make it, while escalation is the behavioral pattern driven by personal responsibility -- managers who personally picked the losing project invest substantially more in it than managers who inherited the same project.
terms.whyItMatters: The structural fix a judge is listening for in a case about a doomed store opening is handing the continue-or-kill call to someone who did not make the original decision; recommending only 'ignore what we already spent' answers the smaller half of the problem.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: Setting price by adding a standard markup to a product's cost.
terms.whyItMatters: It is a foundational method when a price must ensure cost recovery.

terms.definition: The reason a customer buys from this particular seller — service, location, reputation, staff knowledge or credit terms — as distinct from the product motive, which is the reason they want the item from anyone at all. A rep losing on patronage grounds cannot recover the sale by describing the product better.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior exam items sort a list of customer statements into the two motive types, and a roleplay customer who says a competitor is closer to home is testing whether you answer with service instead of features.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: The percentage placed on goods when they first reach the floor, sized to absorb everything that will erode it: (operating expenses + profit + markdowns + employee discounts + shortages) / (net sales + markdowns + discounts + shortages). It is set deliberately higher than maintained markup because none of those reductions have happened yet.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-plan questions ask why a store tickets at 52% when it only expects to keep 40%, and the gap between this figure and maintained markup is the entire answer.

terms.definition: A selling arrangement in which silence counts as a yes — the seller announces the coming shipment and bills unless the buyer declines in time. It is lawful only if the buyer agreed to the terms up front, gets at least 10 days to reject each announced selection, and can cancel through a route as simple as the one used to enroll.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a book or subscription club and ask what makes the automatic shipment legal; a subscription-selling roleplay is scored on disclosing the cancellation route before the customer signs.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: McGregor's paired assumption sets: Theory X holds that workers dislike work and need coercion and close control, while Theory Y holds that work is as natural as rest and that people will self-direct toward goals they are committed to; the manager's assumption becomes self-fulfilling through the controls it justifies.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items quote a supervisor's remark about needing to watch employees constantly and ask which assumption set it reveals and what management style follows.

terms.definition: Paid placement built to match the form and feel of the surrounding editorial content, which the FTC requires be labeled Ad, Sponsored or Paid before the reader clicks — precisely because matching the publisher's format is what stops a reader from telling it apart from unpaid editorial.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay proposing an article that reads like the site's own reporting is scored on whether the competitor puts the disclosure ahead of the click, and exam items contrast it with publicity, which is unpaid and carries no label duty.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Setting a high initial price to earn maximum revenue from eager buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Skimming fits new or innovative products willing buyers will pay for.

terms.definition: Guidance requiring any material connection between an endorser and a seller — payment, free product, a job, a family tie — to be disclosed clearly and right next to the claim rather than buried in a profile or behind a More link, and requiring a testimonial showing unusual results to state what a typical buyer should expect.
terms.whyItMatters: A social-selling roleplay that has you brief an influencer is graded on where the disclosure sits; exam items ask whether a free product with no cash payment still has to be disclosed, and it does.

terms.definition: A business between producer and customer, such as a retailer, wholesaler, or agent.
terms.whyItMatters: Intermediaries expand reach but add cost and control tradeoffs.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: Loyalty points, gift-card balances and promotional credits that were issued but are never redeemed and eventually release to revenue; a program booking 15% and then seeing only 5% has understated its outstanding liability threefold.
terms.whyItMatters: A loyalty-program roleplay asks whether a richer earn rate is affordable, and the answer depends on how much of what is issued is assumed never to be claimed — an assumption that turns into a balance-sheet problem when it is wrong.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: Customers lost during a period divided by customers held at its start, so 240 lost from 4,000 is 6%, with retention rate as its complement at 94%; the figure counts departures and not the revenue those departures carried, so 6% concentrated among the largest accounts damages far more than the percentage implies.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing which measures to monitor for a subscription business, the tested nuance is pairing the customer-count figure with a revenue-weighted view.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: What the retailer actually keeps once reductions are taken: net sales minus gross cost of goods sold, stated as a percent of net sales. It sits below initial markup by the amount of markdowns, shortages and employee discounts, and it - not the original ticket - is the margin that has to cover operating expenses.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance and marketing exams give the initial markup plus a markdown total and ask for the margin that survived, which is this number rather than the one on the price tag.

terms.definition: Months a newly hired rep needs before carrying full quota, credited in steps — commonly no quota in the first quarter, half in the second and full in the third. A rep hired in March therefore contributes roughly a quarter of an annual number that year, which is why headcount added late almost never rescues a current-year gap.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items ask what revenue a mid-year hire adds this year, and the credit schedule is the whole answer; a roleplay on onboarding new sellers expects you to name the stepped quota rather than promise full production on day one.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: A legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law roleplays turn on whether promises, rights, and duties are enforceable.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: A written brief fixing one campaign's target, its single key benefit claim, the support that proves that claim, the tone of voice and the legal mandatories, so that every execution in every medium argues the same one thing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on why the pieces of a campaign must agree points here, and a roleplay presenting a campaign is expected to trace each execution back to the one claim the document fixed.

terms.definition: The moral dimension of a decision dropping out of the frame so it gets processed as a budget, legal or scheduling problem instead. The failure is not a person choosing wrong but a person never seeing a choice, which is why euphemism -- 'aggressive accounting', 'creative sourcing' -- is a diagnostic symptom rather than a cosmetic one. It also explains the prediction gap: in one study most participants said they would refuse or confront an improper interview question, and essentially none did when it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making cases are built on decisions already reframed as operational, and the scoring move is to restore the moral question out loud before analyzing the numbers; competitors who answer only the financial framing lose the ethics indicator entirely.

terms.definition: Rogers' model dividing adopters over time into five fixed bands measured in standard deviations from the mean adoption date — innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34% and laggards 16% — so the opinion-leading early adopters are a narrow 13.5% band that must be won before the 34% early majority will move, and a launch plan aimed at the mass market from day one is aimed at people who are not yet buying.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target first; naming the band and its percentage is what turns 'we'll target trendsetters' into a defensible answer.

terms.definition: Reduction dollars measured against actual net sales rather than against the original ticket: dollar markdown / net sales. The off-retail version instead divides the reduction by the original price, so a $20 cut on a $50 item is a 40% off-retail markdown but a different number in the store's markdown-to-sales figure.
terms.whyItMatters: Clearance-planning roleplays require a candidate to say which denominator they used before a judge will accept the percentage they quote.

terms.definition: A readability formula that grades a passage as 0.4 x (words per sentence + percentage of words carrying three or more syllables), so it counts only 'hard words' instead of weighting every syllable the way Flesch-Kincaid does. On the same paragraph the two scores diverge whenever long sentences are built from plain words: a 40-word sentence of one-syllable words drives fog up sharply while Flesch-Kincaid barely moves. General business writing is normally targeted at 12 or below and news writing near 11.
terms.whyItMatters: An editing item hands you one paragraph and two readability scores and asks which formula flagged it, and a roleplay defending a rewritten warranty is scored on naming a target number rather than promising the draft now 'reads better.'

terms.definition: The sales-tax duty a seller picks up in a state where it owns no building and employs no one, triggered purely by volume — commonly $100,000 of sales or 200 separate transactions into that state in the current or prior year. Cross the threshold and the seller must register, collect and remit there; a purely online business is not exempt.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce selling items give a state-by-state sales table and ask where tax must now be collected; an expansion roleplay expects you to raise registration before recommending a push into a new state.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: A prize promotion whose winners are drawn purely at random, which means it must strip one of the three elements of an illegal lottery — prize, chance and consideration — by publishing a free alternate method of entry so that no purchase is ever necessary.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants entries limited to paying customers is proposing an illegal lottery without realizing it, and the competitor is scored on naming the three elements and the free-entry fix rather than just calling it risky.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Overestimating how much observers notice and later recall one's appearance and actions. Wearers of an embarrassing shirt guessed about half the room could identify it; roughly a quarter could. Unlike the illusion of transparency, the misjudgment is about what is visible on the outside -- a stumble, a stain, an awkward entrance -- rather than about the feelings underneath, and the two are tested as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: Fumbling the first line of a roleplay opener feels catastrophic and costs almost nothing on a judge's rubric; competitors who know the size of the gap recover in one sentence instead of carrying the mistake through the remaining nine minutes.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.
